transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: 2026-04-27
Start: 09:30 AM UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Sofia Martinez (Redwood SE), James Patel (Meridian), Monica Ruiz (Meridian CTO), Evan Lee (Meridian Platform Eng)

Summary:
- Hosted API demo covering chat/text generation basics: streaming, parameters (temperature, max_tokens), retries and idempotency, rate limits.
- Customer cares about latency, cost, and data residency/security; they asked about SSO/KMS and audit logs.
- Agreed next steps: pricing, quickstart code, pilot benchmark.

Topics:
- Streaming responses and how to integrate in frontend
- Parameter tuning (temperature, top_p, max_tokens) and cost impact
- Retry/backoff strategy and idempotency keys
- Rate limiting and usage quotas
- Security: SOC2, SSO, KMS, data retention

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Alex Chen, AE on the account. Sofia from our SE team will run through the demo, then we'll do Q&A.
[00:30] Sofia (Redwood SE): Hi all, yeah thanks. Today we're going to show a quick hosted API demo for chat and text generation basics—streaming, params, and retries. I'll start with a short overview then demo code and the console.
[01:00] James (Meridian): Appreciate it, our main goals are sub-200ms tail latency for short prompts and keeping cost predictable, um, also compliance needs - SSO and KMS.
[01:30] Monica (Meridian CTO): And to add, we have a quarterly audit so audit logs retention is important for us.
[02:00] Sofia: Totally makes sense. Ok, first slide—hosted API. You can call /v1/chat or /v1/text, streaming supported via server-sent events. Note: we support chunked streaming and incremental deltas.
[03:00] Alex: Quick note on pricing model, it's per-token for generation and per-embedding unit; we'll follow up with a detailed TCO for your expected qps.
[04:00] Evan (Meridian): Do you have client libraries? We prefer node and python SDKs.
[05:00] Sofia: Yep, we have SDKs. I'll share a sample streaming client in both node and python after the call. The streaming part looks like this—(reviews code) you open a connection and then receive events with partial text.
[06:00] Sofia: One caveat—network glitches can cause broken streams, so we recommend idempotency keys on requests and resumable streaming in the client. Our hosted API accepts an idempotency_key header.
[07:00] James: Can you explain the retry semantics? If we retry, do we double-charge or get duplicate tokens?
[08:00] Sofia: Good question—retries with the same idempotency key are deduplicated server-side. If a request times out client-side and you retry with same key, we either return the cached response or start a new request depending on state. There's a short window for dedupe; we'll share docs with exact timings.
[09:00] Alex: Also we recommend exponential backoff with jitter; Example: 200ms, 500ms, 1s with jitter for transient 5xx errors.
[10:00] Monica: What about rate limits? We expect bursts during batch billing runs.
[11:00] Sofia: We expose rate limits in headers and on the console per API key. You can set quotas and alerts. For bursts, consider request shaping or a dedicated plan if predictable throughput is needed.
[12:00] Evan: Any differences between hosted vs. dedicated for latency? We might need more consistent tail latency.
[13:00] Alex: Hosted is great for time-to-value; Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools and better predictable tail latency but costs more. We'll run a TCO comparison.
[14:00] James: For streaming, do you stream tokens or deltas with structured output? We need to interleave tool calls.
[15:00] Sofia: We stream deltas; you can send function/tool calls and we support structured JSON chunks as well. Small caveat some transcriptions show up as 'function call' tokenization differences, but we support function calling in streaming.
[16:00] James: How about prompt engineering—do you have guidance for temperature and top_p for short financial prompts?
[17:00] Sofia: For deterministic outputs, lower temperature (0–0.2) and lower top_p (0.8) helps. Also keep max_tokens tight to control cost. We can share a short playbook.
[18:00] Alex: I'll include our prompt playbook and example prompts for accounting and report generation.
[19:00] Monica: Security—do you support SAML SSO and SCIM? We use Okta.
[20:00] Alex: Yes, SSO via SAML + SCIM provisioning is supported for enterprise customers; we'll share the setup guide. KMS integrations for customer-managed keys are supported in Private and Dedicated; for Hosted we offer envelope encryption with our KMS and can support BYOK for enterprise contracts.
[21:00] Evan: How about audit logs? Do you retain raw request/response or just headers?
[22:00] Sofia: We can surface audit logs with request metadata; raw PII is redacted by default in hosted, but we can configure retention windows and longer retention for enterprise add-ons.
[23:00] James: Any limits on token size or context window? We deal with docs up to 10k tokens.
[24:00] Sofia: Our largest hosted models support up to 32k tokens; cost scales with context. For heavy long-context workloads we sometimes recommend retrieval augmented generation and caching.
[25:00] Alex: Quick demo now—Sofia will run the console and a streaming example.
[26:00] Sofia: (shares screen) Here's the Console—API keys, model catalog, streaming logs. I'll trigger a streaming chat with temperature 0.1 and max_tokens 150.
[27:00] [screen demo noise] Sofia: You can see partial deltas appearing in the client, then final delta. This shows reduced latency since we send tokens as they're generated.
[28:00] James: Nice, latency looks ok in demo. In production our network to your region might add 30–40ms.
[29:00] Sofia: We also provide regional endpoints and edge routing to reduce RTT.
[30:00] Evan: On retries—if we get a 429, what's the recommended flow?
[31:00] Alex: For 429, use standard retry-after header and exponential backoff; we also expose per-key quota so you can apply backpressure client-side.
[32:00] Monica: For compliance, can we get SOC2 and penetration testing reports?
[33:00] Alex: Yes we'll share SOC2 and security whitepapers; penetration test summary for enterprise package.
[34:00] Sofia: Also note we have built-in observability: per-request token counts, latency percentiles and tracing hooks to link back to your traces.
[35:00] James: How do we handle streaming reconnections? If client loses socket, can we reconnect and continue from last token?
[36:00] Sofia: Currently we provide idempotency and resumable tokens in the SDK examples; full byte-range resume is in roadmap but we can implement more robust resumable streaming in dedicated pilots.
[37:00] Alex: Ok, time check—about 30 minutes in, do you want to dive deeper into any area?
[38:00] James: We'd like a short pilot to validate latency and cost. Can we get a 2-week pilot with some traffic replay?
[39:00] Alex: Yes, we can do a pilot; we'll scope the exact qps and dataset. Evan, can you provide sample load/profile?
[40:00] Evan: Sure, I'll share expected qps, typical prompt sizes and peak windows by tomorrow.
[41:00] Monica: We'll need security docs and the pricing to present to procurement.
[42:00] Alex: We'll send pricing + security docs. Sofia will send quickstart and streaming samples.
[43:00] James: Any known issues with financial language models and hallucinations on numeric data?
[44:00] Sofia: Hallucinations are a risk—recommended mitigations: grounding with retrieval, post-hoc verification, and token limits. Also ensemble prompts can help.

End of transcript.
